plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true story of 1816, the 'year without a summer': snow falls in Vermont in June, rain traps Lord Byron's guests at the Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva, Byron sets a ghost-story contest and 18-year-old Mary Godwin, stuck for days, sees Frankenstein's creature in a waking dream; the twist is that the cold summer itself was caused by the eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia a year earlier.

script.title: The Cold Summer That Made a Monster

beats.say: 1816, Lake Geneva. Summer never came, and a monster was born.
A monster? Born in summer? Mothwick, monsters aren't born.
Her name was Mary. She was eighteen, and she could not sleep.
This one is true, Odo. She wrote it all down herself.
That June, rain fell almost every day. The sky stayed grey.
When the sun did show, it looked dim and strangely red.
A red sun in June? That's not a normal summer.
Across the ocean, in Vermont, snow fell in early June.
My corn froze in the field. In June, I tell you.
Frost came back in July, and again in August.
New Englanders called it Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.
In Europe the harvests failed. Bread ran short. People went hungry.
But why? Why did a whole summer just disappear?
Nobody knew. By the lake, Lord Byron had rented the Villa Diodati.
Mary, her future husband Percy Shelley, and Doctor John Polidori came.
It proved a wet, ungenial summer. Rain kept us inside for days.
By candlelight, they read a book of German ghost stories aloud.
We will each write a ghost story. Every one of us.
A ghost story contest, in a storm? I would hide.
Byron began one. Polidori began one. Percy began one.
Every morning they asked if I had a story. I had nothing.
Days passed, Odo. She was sure she would fail.
One night, the men talked late about the spark of life.
Scientists had made dead frogs' legs twitch with electricity.
Frogs? Mothwick, I don't like where this is going.
Subscribe for a new true story every day. Now the strangest night.
Mary went to bed long after midnight. She could not sleep.
With my eyes shut, I saw a pale student kneeling.
Beside him lay a thing he had put together.
Then the thing opened its yellow, watery eyes.
I opened my own eyes in terror. And then I knew.
The next morning she told them: I have found my story.
It became Frankenstein, published in London in January 1818.
Eighteen years old, Odo, and she changed horror stories forever.
So the storm made the story. But what made the storm?
That July, Byron wrote a black poem. He called it Darkness.
I had a dream, which was not all a dream.
Polidori finished The Vampyre, one of the first vampire stories in English.
One cold summer, Odo. Two monsters. And still nobody knew why.
The answer was a year old, and half a world away.
April 1815. Mount Tambora, in today's Indonesia, exploded.
The biggest eruption in recorded history threw ash high into the sky.
That fine haze spread around the whole planet, Odo.
So it dimmed the sunlight. That's why the sun looked red!
Yes. Scientists linked the lost summer to Tambora about a century later.
Mary never knew that a volcano helped wake her monster.
A mountain blew up, and a monster woke up in Geneva.
If this one got you, the Tunguska sky blast story is next.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: 1816: A Cold Summer Made a Monster | True Story Animated
long.description:
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/mDtBUZwlwHU
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

"A mountain blew up, and a monster woke up in Geneva." — Odo

A true story from 1816, the year without a summer: snow fell in Vermont in June, and endless rain trapped Lord Byron, Percy Shelley, John Polidori and 18-year-old Mary Godwin at the Villa Diodati on Lake Geneva. Byron dared them each to write a ghost story, and one sleepless night Mary saw the creature that became Frankenstein. Nobody then knew why the summer had vanished: the eruption of Mount Tambora, a year earlier and half a world away.
